full_judgment: 4. The writ petition was opposed by Enemy Property Authority principally on two grounds; first: that the Partnership between Respondents and Chiranjib Lal Saraf did not constitute a bonafide or a valid partnership; secondly, Chiranjib left East Pakistan in February, 1968, and settled in Calcutta and so became an enemy subject. The firm became an enemy firm, and the property, held by it, enemy property. A Bench of the Dacca High Court, on bearing the parties, allowed the writ petition, holding firstly: that the respondents had proved their prima facie title, and so their possession was not unauthorized secondly, there was no sufficient evidence to hold that Chiranjib left Pakistan and permanently settled in India, and hence presumption remains that his domicile of origin never ceased, and so the Firm, and the property held by it, were immune from the mischief of Defense of Pakistan Ordinance and the Rules framed thereunder; and thirdly, the deed of transfer in favor of Chiranjib was not hit by provisions of Disturbed Persons Ordinance.
